input.question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?
input.ground_truth: The main reason is that electricity usage is highest during heat waves, because everyone's air conditioning is running at full blast. There's a second less important reason, which is that fossil fuel and nuclear power plants are less efficient in hot weather. They use outside air and/or water to cool their steam back to water to recycle back into the plant, and that doesn't work as well on a hot day. In fact, it turns out there's a theorem of thermodynamics that says that the maximum possible efficiency of both heat engines (power plant) and refrigerators (air conditioners) is worse when the outside air is warmer. _URL_0_

Question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big toy box full of toys, but it’s super, super hot outside. When it’s really hot, everything gets hot—even the big machines that help give us electricity (we call them “power plants”).

These machines work really hard to keep the lights on, but when it’s extremely hot, they get tired and sometimes don’t work as well. Also, the wires that bring electricity to your house can get so hot that they droop or even break a little bit, like how a melted chocolate bar can’t hold its shape.

When the machines get too hot or the wires get too wobbly, they can’t carry the electricity to your house, so the lights go out for lots of people at the same time. That’s called a “blackout.”

So, when it’s super hot, the electricity machines and wires get too hot and tired, and that can make the power go out for many people!
